summary: This specification defines a profile of OCSP that tackles scalability in large PKI environments and in those needing a lightweight solution with low communication overhead. It obsoletes RFC 5019.

eli5.summary: Checking if a certificate is still good can swamp a server when millions ask. This is a slimmed-down way to answer so it scales.

questions: what is the lightweight ocsp profile
when should an ocsp client use http get
subtitle: How to slim down and cache OCSP certificate-status checks so they scale to millions of users.

tldr.problem: Plain OCSP can force a responder to build a fresh signed answer for every request, which does not scale in very large PKIs or on bandwidth-limited, low-power clients.
tldr.mechanism: The profile restricts OCSP messages to one small request, lets responders pre-produce and sign answers with a nextUpdate time, uses HTTP GET so caches can help, and requires SHA-256 for CertID hashes.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5019, whose profile required SHA-1. Clients that still use SHA-1 for compatibility must move to SHA-256 as soon as practical.

today: RFC 9919 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5019, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It carries the lightweight OCSP profile forward with SHA-256 in place of SHA-1.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight OCSP Profile
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) defined in RFC 6960 lets a client check the status of a digital certificate instead of downloading a Certificate Revocation List (CRL). Many deployments have required responders to answer in real time, generating a new response for each request, and have assumed plenty of bandwidth and processing power.

That does not scale to PKIs with millions or hundreds of millions of certificates, or to mobile settings where bandwidth is at a premium and clients are constrained. This document defines a message profile and clarifies client and responder behavior to permit three things: OCSP response pre-production and distribution, reduced message size to lower bandwidth, and response caching in the network and on the client.

OCSP has no way to signal responder capabilities, so clients may need out-of-band arrangements to know whether a responder follows this profile. Interoperability still holds between a fully RFC 6960 client and a responder operating in this mode.
sections.eli5: When too many people ask the same question, the answerer gets swamped. This profile is a plan so that the answers can be prepared ahead and shared.

sections.title: The Request and Response Profile
sections.content:
A conforming OCSPRequest MUST include only one Request in its requestList. Clients MUST use SHA-256 for the issuerNameHash and issuerKeyHash in the CertID. Older clients that stay compatible with RFC 5019 use SHA-1 but MUST transition to SHA-256 as soon as practical. Clients MUST NOT include singleRequestExtensions and SHOULD NOT include requestExtensions; if they do, only the nonce extension is recommended. Clients SHOULD NOT send signed requests, and responders MAY ignore the signature.

A responder MUST generate a BasicOCSPResponse. Responses SHOULD contain one SingleResponse, but MAY contain more, for example one CertID using SHA-1 and one using SHA-256 for clients not yet using SHA-256. Responders SHOULD NOT distribute SHA-1 CertIDs if no clients need them. Clients MUST validate the response signature. A delegated responder certificate MUST be included in the certs field, SHOULD carry the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension and should be short-lived. New responders MUST identify themselves with the byKey field to keep responses small.

If the responder has no authoritative record for a certificate, it MUST return the status unauthorized. When pre-producing responses, nextUpdate MUST be present, to help caching. The times thisUpdate, nextUpdate and producedAt MUST be GMT (Zulu), include seconds and not include fractions, in the form YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ.
sections.eli5: The question is kept short, one certificate at a time. The answer is a signed note that says what is true, when it was true, and when a newer note will come out.

sections.title: How Clients Behave
sections.content:
Clients MUST support the Authority Information Access (AIA) extension and recognize the id-ad-ocsp access method to find the responder. If a certificate points to both an OCSP responder and a CRL, the client SHOULD try the responder first, and MAY fetch the CRL if no response arrives after a locally configured timeout and number of retries.

To avoid needless traffic, an application MUST verify the signature on signed data, and on the certificates in a chain, before asking for an OCSP check; if a signature is invalid, an OCSP check MUST NOT be requested. Clients SHOULD NOT request the status of expired certificates.
sections.eli5: Before you ask whether a library card is valid, first check that the card is not obviously fake or already expired. No point wasting the librarian's time.

sections.title: Keeping Responses Fresh
sections.content:
A client must make sure it does not accept an out-of-date response saying good when a newer one says revoked. Two mechanisms exist: nonces and time. Because the profile says clients SHOULD NOT send request extensions, clients MUST be able to judge freshness from an accurate source of time, and responders need one too.

A client MUST check that nextUpdate exists and that the current time falls between thisUpdate and nextUpdate. A response without nextUpdate MUST be rejected, and so must one that is stale. Clients MAY allow a small tolerance period after nextUpdate for clock differences; the text suggests a client with no NTP analogue might allow, for example, one day.

A client that sent a nonce SHOULD NOT reject a response solely because the nonce is missing, but MUST fall back to time-based validation. A client that did not send a nonce MUST ignore any nonce in the response.
sections.eli5: An answer note has a use-by date. If today is past that date, throw the note away and ask again.

sections.title: HTTP Transport
sections.content:
The responder MUST support OCSP over HTTP. When a request is 255 bytes or less in total, including the http:// scheme, server name and base64-encoded request, clients MUST use the GET method so that responses can be cached. Larger requests SHOULD use POST. For GET, the request is base64-encoded, with no whitespace or other characters outside the base64 repertoire, URL-encoded, and appended to the URI from the AIA extension.

A cachable response carries the DER-encoded OCSP response preceded by header fields such as Content-type: application/ocsp-response, Content-length, Last-modified, ETag, Expires, Cache-control and Date.
sections.eli5: Short questions go in the address of a web link so that helpful shops along the way can remember the answer. Longer questions are handed over in a package that cannot be remembered the same way.

sections.title: Caching Rules
sections.content:
Clients MUST locally cache authoritative responses, meaning those with a valid signature and a status of successful. To avoid spikes when many clients refresh a popular certificate at nextUpdate, responders MAY set cache-control:max-age, clients SHOULD fetch a fresh response on or after that time, and responders MUST refresh the response before the max-age time.

On the HTTP side, Last-Modified matches thisUpdate, Expires matches nextUpdate, and the ETag is recommended to be the ASCII hex of the SHA-256 hash of the response. The Cache-Control directives are max-age, public, no-transform and must-revalidate. Authoritative responses MUST NOT include Pragma: no-cache, Cache-Control: no-cache or Cache-Control: no-store. Clients MUST NOT send no-cache in requests, unless they meet an expired response, when they SHOULD retry with a no-cache header to bypass stale proxies.

The profile also discusses including OCSP responses in a protocol exchange, called stapling. It lets servers cache responses, lets clients validate offline, reduces round trips in a handshake and simplifies the client. TLS clients and servers are RECOMMENDED to implement the certificate status request extension.
sections.eli5: If everyone keeps a copy of the notice and only looks for a new one when the old one runs out, the answerer is asked far less often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These add to the considerations in RFC 6960. Since nonces are optional here, an old response could be replayed, so clients MUST have an accurate clock and check freshness; a client with a clock that is too fast may reject fresh responses, and one that is too slow may accept expired ones. To resist on-path and impersonation attacks, clients MUST validate response signatures and confirm the signer is authorized.

Because requests are unsigned, anyone can send them, so responders SHOULD defend against denial of service, for example by rate limiting an IP address. HTTP header values are not cryptographically protected, so clients should use them only as caching hints and rely on the signed response, and SHOULD NOT rely on a cached response beyond nextUpdate.

The use of SHA-1 for CertID hashes is not a cryptographic concern as such, but keeping it forces software to keep SHA-1 support, which increases complexity and attack surface.
sections.eli5: The use-by date and the signature on the note are what you trust, not the sticker on the envelope, because anyone could change the sticker.

sections.title: Differences From RFC 5019
sections.content:
RFC 5019 mandated SHA-1 for several fields. Because weaknesses in SHA-1 have been demonstrated, RFC 9919 recommends SHA-256 where SHA-1 was required. An RFC 5019 client can still use SHA-1, but that may become obsolete.

The substantive changes are: new clients must use SHA-256, new responders must use the byKey field, and clients MUST NOT include whitespace or other non-base64 characters in the base64-encoded GET string.
sections.eli5: The old rule used a lock that people now know is weak. The new rule says to use a stronger lock for new things.
